questions.q: What is the key difference between ETL and ELT in a modern data pipeline?
options: ETL transforms data before it lands in the destination; ELT loads raw data into the destination first and transforms it there using the destination's own compute
ETL is used only for streaming data; ELT is used only for batch data
ETL and ELT both transform data in the source system before extraction
ELT is an older pattern that ADF no longer supports
questions.explain: ETL does transformation work before loading, which mattered when destinations had limited compute; ELT flips the order so raw data lands first and the destination's own powerful engine (a cloud warehouse or Spark) does the transforming, which scales better for large volumes.

questions.q: What is Azure Data Factory, fundamentally?
options: A relational database engine for storing transactional data
A cloud-based data integration service for building and orchestrating data pipelines that move and transform data at scale
A programming language for writing stored procedures
A visualization tool for building dashboards
questions.explain: ADF doesn't store or process data itself — it's an orchestration layer that connects to sources and sinks, coordinates activities like Copy and Data Flows, and schedules pipeline runs.

questions.q: What is the relationship between a Linked Service and a Dataset in Azure Data Factory?
options: A Dataset defines the connection string; a Linked Service defines which table to read
They are interchangeable and either one can be used for both purposes
A Linked Service defines the connection information to a data store; a Dataset points to a specific piece of data (like a table or file path) within that connected store
A Linked Service can only be used with Mapping Data Flows, never with Copy Activity
questions.explain: The Linked Service holds connection details such as server and credentials; the Dataset then points to a specific structure — a table, container, or file — inside that connection, so many Datasets can reuse one Linked Service.

questions.q: Why would you parameterize a Linked Service instead of creating a separate Linked Service for every database on the same server?
options: Parameterization is required by Azure before any pipeline can run
It removes the need to configure authentication entirely
Parameterized Linked Services can only connect to Blob Storage
It lets one Linked Service dynamically connect to different databases or servers at runtime, avoiding the need to duplicate near-identical connections
questions.explain: Parameterizing lets one Linked Service and Dataset pair serve many similar sources by passing in values like server or database name at runtime, avoiding factory sprawl from near-duplicate connections.

questions.q: What does the Copy Activity do in an Azure Data Factory pipeline?
options: It moves data from a source dataset to a sink (destination) dataset, optionally mapping columns along the way, without applying complex transformation logic
It only duplicates a pipeline for testing purposes
It always converts data to Parquet format
It runs arbitrary Python or Spark code against the data
questions.explain: Copy Activity is built for efficient bulk movement between a source and sink with light column mapping; real row-level transformation logic belongs in a Mapping Data Flow or similar compute activity.

questions.q: In the context of Copy Activity, what does 'schema drift' refer to?
options: A bug where the pipeline silently deletes the destination table
Source data whose columns change or vary between runs (added, removed, or reordered columns) that the pipeline needs to tolerate without breaking
The delay between when data is extracted and when it's loaded
A setting that forces all columns to be cast to strings
questions.explain: Schema drift means the source's columns can change between runs; a pipeline built to tolerate drift keeps working even when upstream systems add, remove, or reorder columns.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Parameter and a Variable in an Azure Data Factory pipeline?
options: Parameters can only hold numbers; variables can only hold strings
Variables are passed in at pipeline start; parameters change during execution
A parameter's value is passed in when the pipeline starts and cannot be changed during the run; a variable is set inside the pipeline and can be updated as activities execute
There is no functional difference — they are just different names for the same object
questions.explain: Parameters are fixed once a pipeline run starts, ideal for values passed in from a trigger; variables are mutable and get updated mid-run with Set Variable or Append Variable, often for counters or accumulators.

questions.q: What does the ForEach activity do in Azure Data Factory?
options: It repeats a single activity forever until the pipeline is manually stopped
It merges the results of multiple pipelines into one dataset
It is only usable inside a Mapping Data Flow, not a pipeline
It iterates over a collection (such as an array of file names) and runs its inner activities once for each item, optionally in parallel
questions.explain: ForEach is ADF's loop construct: given an array, often from a Lookup or Get Metadata activity, it runs its inner activities once per item, sequentially or in parallel up to a batch limit.

questions.q: What engine actually executes a Mapping Data Flow when you run it in Azure Data Factory?
options: A Spark cluster spun up behind the scenes, which ADF abstracts away behind a visual, code-free drag-and-drop interface
The same lightweight Integration Runtime used by Copy Activity
A T-SQL execution engine inside Azure SQL Database
Your local machine running the Data Factory Studio browser tab
questions.explain: Mapping Data Flows compile their visual transformation graph into Spark jobs run on managed clusters behind the scenes, which is why turning on Debug Mode has a noticeable cluster warm-up delay.

questions.q: What does the Derived Column transformation do in a Mapping Data Flow?
options: It removes duplicate rows from the incoming stream
It creates a new column (or overwrites an existing one) by applying an expression, such as a calculation or string manipulation, to each row
It joins two streams together based on a matching key
It splits one stream into multiple streams based on a condition
questions.explain: Derived Column is the general per-row compute transformation — you write an expression and it either adds a new column or overwrites an existing one with the result.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Conditional Split transformation in a Mapping Data Flow?
options: It splits a single row into multiple rows
It divides a large file into smaller files for parallel processing
It routes each incoming row down one of several output streams based on which condition it matches first, similar to a switch statement
It cancels the data flow if more than one condition is true
questions.explain: Conditional Split evaluates each row against an ordered list of conditions and routes it to the first matching output stream, letting you branch pipeline logic much like a switch statement.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a Schedule Trigger and a Tumbling Window Trigger in Azure Data Factory?
options: A Tumbling Window Trigger can only be used with Mapping Data Flows
A Schedule Trigger cannot run more than once per day
Tumbling Window Triggers are deprecated in favor of Schedule Triggers

A Schedule Trigger just fires a pipeline at fixed times with no memory of past runs; a Tumbling Window Trigger fires over fixed, non-overlapping time windows and can retry, track dependencies, and reprocess a specific past window
questions.explain: Tumbling Window Triggers process fixed time slices and carry built-in retry and dependency-chaining between windows, plus the ability to reprocess one specific historical window — none of which a plain Schedule Trigger offers.

questions.q: When do you need a Self-Hosted Integration Runtime instead of the Azure Integration Runtime?
options: When your pipeline needs to reach data sources that live on-premises or inside a private network not reachable directly from the public internet
When you want to run a Mapping Data Flow, since Mapping Data Flows require self-hosted compute
When your data volume exceeds 1 GB
Self-hosted Integration Runtimes are only for scheduling triggers, not for moving data
questions.explain: The Azure IR runs in Microsoft's managed network and can't reach into a private network; a Self-Hosted IR is installed on a machine inside that network to act as a secure bridge for on-premises sources.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a retry policy on an Azure Data Factory activity?
options: It permanently disables the activity after its first failure
It automatically re-attempts a failed activity a specified number of times with a delay between attempts, which helps the pipeline recover from transient failures like a brief network blip
It duplicates every successful run for backup purposes
It changes the activity's timeout to unlimited
questions.explain: Many failures are transient — a brief network blip or a momentary throttling response — so an automatic retry with a delay often succeeds on the next attempt instead of failing the whole pipeline.

questions.q: How does a Fabric Dataflow Gen2 differ from an Azure Data Factory Mapping Data Flow?
options: Dataflow Gen2 can only read from Excel files
Mapping Data Flows run inside Fabric, while Dataflow Gen2 only runs inside classic ADF
Dataflow Gen2 is built on Power Query (the same M-language engine used in Power BI and Excel) rather than the Spark-based visual transformation engine behind Mapping Data Flows
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explain: Dataflow Gen2 runs on the Power Query/M engine familiar from Power BI and Excel, while Mapping Data Flows compile to Spark jobs — different engines aimed at similar transformation problems.

questions.q: What role does OneLake play when a Fabric pipeline uses it as a destination?
options: OneLake is a temporary staging area that gets deleted after each pipeline run
OneLake only stores pipeline execution logs, not actual data
OneLake requires a separate Azure subscription from the rest of Fabric

OneLake acts as a single, tenant-wide data lake (built on ADLS Gen2 and Delta format) that all Fabric workloads share, so writing there makes the data usable across Lakehouses, Warehouses, and Power BI without copying it
questions.explain: Every Fabric workspace gets a shared OneLake location automatically; data landed there in Delta format is immediately visible to other Fabric engines like the Lakehouse SQL endpoint or Power BI Direct Lake without a separate copy.

questions.q: Why is using a Managed Identity together with Key Vault considered a security best practice in Azure Data Factory, instead of hardcoding a connection string with a password?
options: It lets ADF authenticate to resources and retrieve secrets without any credential ever being stored in plain text inside a Linked Service definition or source code
It makes pipelines run faster because passwords slow down authentication
Key Vault is required before a pipeline can be published to Git
Managed Identities remove the need for RBAC entirely
questions.explain: A Managed Identity lets ADF authenticate to Key Vault and other services without any stored credential, and Key Vault then holds the remaining secrets ADF does need — keeping passwords out of Linked Service JSON entirely.

questions.q: In Azure Data Factory's Git integration, what is the purpose of publishing to the adf_publish branch?
options: adf_publish is where developers write and save their day-to-day pipeline edits
Publishing compiles the collaboration (feature) branch's JSON into ARM templates and deploys them to the live Data Factory service, separate from the branch you were actively editing in
Publishing deletes the collaboration branch after deployment
adf_publish only stores documentation, never pipeline definitions
questions.explain: In Git mode you author against a collaboration branch, but nothing runs live until Publish generates ARM templates into adf_publish and deploys them — separating source-controlled authoring from what's actually live.

questions.q: In a capstone pipeline that needs to keep running even if one Copy Activity fails, which control-flow pattern lets you branch based on that activity's outcome?
options: Adding a Wait activity before the Copy Activity
Increasing the Copy Activity's degree of copy parallelism

Connecting a downstream activity to the failed activity's 'Failure' output path (or wrapping it in an If Condition checking activity status), so error-handling logic runs specifically when that step fails
Renaming the pipeline
questions.explain: ADF models success and failure as separate output paths from an activity, so attaching a downstream activity to the 'On Failure' path gives you try/catch-like error handling without writing code.

questions.q: When designing an end-to-end pipeline, when should you reach for a Mapping Data Flow instead of a plain Copy Activity?
options: Whenever the source and destination are in the same Azure region
Copy Activity should never be used if a Mapping Data Flow is available
Only when the pipeline has more than 10 activities
When the data needs actual row-level transformation logic — joins, aggregations, conditional routing, derived calculations — beyond just moving and column-mapping it from source to sink
questions.explain: Copy Activity excels at high-throughput movement with light mapping; once you need joins, aggregations, or conditional routing at the row level, a Mapping Data Flow's Spark-backed engine is the right tool.
